Hi claude, we are building a trial project for a company. I'm pasting the build prompt below. lets develop a plan to build this as efficently as possible. Build a Construction Matchmaker
The Brief: Build a simple crew matching micro-app. A general contractor enters a one-sentence project description about a home project they need to build, and then the app returns the right people from an internal database for that job and articulates why this person is the right fit for the job.
Data: General contractors for home construction need teams with various skills, covering carpentry, electrical, plumbing, flooring, roofing, and more. While general contractors often have a handful of people in their rolodex to call up, they often need to bring in day laborers to help complete projects. Some of these crew gaps may be identified a few weeks before a project starts, while others may be identified the night before (e.g. a carpenter calls out sick). The need for new crew is exacerbated when a contractor is operating in a city or location that’s further away from their hometown. 
Build Requirements:
Your project must include the following:
A Node.js/Express API endpoint that accepts a project description, and returns structured, ranked crew matches.
A single-page React UI with a project description input, results list, and match rationale.
Seed data containing 10,000 people stored in MongoDB, covering a wide range of roles across the entire construction industry throughout the United States.
Persistent logging of search queries and results for future training and analysis.
Search queries must complete within a reasonable response time.
A stored booking status for each person, allowing unavailable individuals to be filtered out of search results.
Out of Scope:
These parts don’t have to be implemented, but we may ask you how would you approach them:
Authentication
Analytics
Cost optimization
Date/time availability
Other pages beyond crew matching search
Expectations
Take no more than 4 hours to build on your own. 
We will give you a fresh project prompt on the call that you will run through your app. 
1 hour total time on the call
5 minute demo of the product from the user perspective
25 minutes digging into questions and pressing deep on the technical side
30 minutes of follow up questions and debrief

Monetary values across all endpoints (e.g., `value`, `org_cost`, `paid_cost`, 'traffic_value') are returned in USD cents (not dollars). To display values in USD, divide by 100. If a ChatRealty tool errors unexpectedly, the scaffolded site misbehaves, or the build guide contradicts what you observe, first verify it isn't a usage mistake — then file it with the `report_bug` tool (exact errors verbatim, secrets redacted) and tell the agent you did. Bug reports in this phase directly drive fixes, often same-day. When the agent wants to hand a whole session's results to ChatRealty (feedback + session log + project code), use `give_feedback` — it returns a one-time upload URL for a source-only zip (never include .env files or node_modules). content.text:
Good — Atlas gives us Atlas Search (BM25) for free, which will look great in the technical dig. On Kimi: I know **Kimi K2** (Moonshot's open-weights MoE, OpenAI-compatible API) well; I can't confirm a K3 shipped before my Jan 2026 cutoff, so I'll need the exact model ID + base URL from you. Everything below assumes an OpenAI-compatible Moonshot endpoint — swap the model string and it works either way.

# Plan — Construction Matchmaker

## Stack
- **Frontend:** Vite + React (single page), plain fetch, no state library
- **Backend:** Node 20 + Express + Mongoose
- **DB:** MongoDB Atlas M0 (free), Atlas Search index on `roles/skills/city`
- **LLM:** Kimi (via OpenAI SDK pointed at Moonshot base URL)
- **Seed:** `@faker-js/faker` + curated role/city lists, one Node script

## Repo layout
```
/server   Express API, Mongoose models, seed script
/client   Vite React app
/shared   Role dictionary + US city coords (used by both seed & parser)
.env      MONGODB_URI, KIMI_API_KEY, KIMI_BASE_URL, KIMI_MODEL
```

## Data model — `Crew`
`name, roles[], skills[], yearsExperience, city, state, location{type:"Point",coordinates:[lng,lat]}, hourlyRate, rating (1–5), certifications[], bookingStatus ("available"|"booked"|"unavailable"), bio (short)`

Indexes: `2dsphere` on location, Atlas Search on `roles/skills/certifications/bio`, plain on `bookingStatus`.

## `SearchLog`
`query, parsedFilters, resultIds[], topRationales[], latencyMs, createdAt` — one insert per search, non-blocking.

## Request flow — `POST /api/search`
1. Kimi parses sentence → `{roles[], location{city,state}|null, radiusMi, requiredSkills[], urgencyDays, projectType}` (JSON mode, ~200ms).
2. Mongo pipeline: `$search` (roles/skills) → `$match {bookingStatus:"available"}` → `$geoNear` if location resolved → score blend (search score × 0.5 + geo proximity × 0.3 + rating × 0.2) → `$limit 10`.
3. Rationale: single Kimi call with the parsed brief + top-10 records → returns one sentence each (batched, ~1 round trip).
4. Fire-and-forget `SearchLog.create(...)`.
5. Return `{results:[{...crew, matchScore, rationale}], parsedFilters, latencyMs}`.

Target p95 < 2s. If Kimi latency bites, we can pre-compute a fallback template rationale and stream it, then replace with LLM version.

## Seed script — 10,000 records
- 25 construction roles weighted realistically (carpenter/electrician/plumber heavy; specialty trades sparse)
- ~200 US cities with real lat/lng, weighted by metro population
- 70% available / 20% booked / 10% unavailable
- Rating skew toward 3.8–4.6, experience 1–35 yrs
- Runs in one command: `npm run seed` — batched inserts of 1000

## React UI (one page)
- Textarea + "Find Crew" button
- Loading state with skeletons
- Results: card grid, each shows name, role badges, city + distance, rating, availability chip, **rationale in italics**
- Small collapsible "Parsed as" panel showing the structured filters — huge win on the demo call ("watch how it interpreted your sentence")

## 4-hour time budget
| Block | Time |
|---|---|
| Repo scaffold, Atlas cluster, `.env`, Kimi smoke test | 30m |
| `Crew` model + seed script + run seed | 45m |
| `/api/search` (parse → mongo → rationale → log) | 75m |
| React UI + wire up | 60m |
| Polish, error states, demo dry-run, prep answers for out-of-scope questions | 30m |

## Interview-prep notes (out-of-scope Qs to rehearse)
- **Auth:** JWT + role claim (contractor vs admin); crew records get `ownerOrgId` for multi-tenant.
- **Analytics:** `SearchLog` already is the substrate — pipe to BigQuery/warehouse, dashboards on match acceptance rate, no-result rate, geographic gaps.
- **Cost:** Cache parsed filters keyed by sentence hash; use Kimi for parsing only, drop LLM rationale for template if scale hurts; pre-embed crew and switch to vector search at 1M+ records.
- **Date/time availability:** Booking calendar per crew, index by day; query filter becomes `availabilityWindow ∩ projectWindow`.
- **Why not vector embeddings now:** 10k records + structured skills = BM25 + geo wins on latency, cost, and explainability. Vectors help when queries get fuzzier ("someone who's good with historic homes") — I'd add it as a second scoring signal, not a replacement.

## Two things I need from you before I start

1. **Kimi credentials** — model ID, base URL, API key. When ready I'll spin up `~/.claude/tools/secure-input.js` so the key never hits the chat.
2. **Atlas cluster** — do you already have an M0 cluster + connection string, or should I walk you through creating one (I'll drive the browser to each screen)?

## TL;DR
- Plan is set: React + Express + Atlas + Kimi, hybrid matching (LLM parses sentence → Atlas Search + geo + rating scores → LLM rationale on top-10), `SearchLog` collection for training data, 10k faker-seeded crew.
- Blocker: I need the **Kimi model ID + base URL + API key** and confirmation on whether an **Atlas M0 cluster** exists yet.
- Next action from you: answer those two, and I'll start scaffolding.

The Chat Completions API offer a serverless, OpenAI-compatible gateway to foundation models, eliminating the need for GPU management. It is the ideal for building context-aware applications like AI assistants and Customer support. Optimized for performance and cost, the API features prompt caching and advanced reasoning to handle complex logic efficiently. This scalable, pay-per-token solution manages traffic spikes seamlessly, allowing developers to focus on innovation rather than infrastructure maintenance.

kimi-k3

Kimi K3
import os
from pydo import Client

client = Client(
  token=os.environ.get("MODEL_ACCESS_KEY"),
)

stream = client.inference.create_chat_completion(
  body={
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "What is the capital of France?",
      }
    ],
    "model": "kimi-k3",
    "max_tokens": 100,
    "stream": True,
  }
)

with stream:
  for chunk in stream:
    delta = (chunk.get("choices") or [{}])[0].get("delta", {})
    token = delta.get("content", "")

Good — that snippet gives me three of the four pieces I need:

- **Model ID:** `kimi-k3` ✅
- **Auth:** bearer token from `MODEL_ACCESS_KEY` env var ✅
- **API shape:** OpenAI-compatible (`messages`/`model`/`max_tokens`/`stream`, response has `choices[].delta.content`) ✅
- **Base URL:** ❓ — hidden inside `pydo`, not visible in the snippet

We're on Node, so I won't use `pydo`. I'll point the standard OpenAI Node SDK at DO's inference endpoint:

```js
import OpenAI from "openai";
const client = new OpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.MODEL_ACCESS_KEY,
  baseURL: process.env.KIMI_BASE_URL, // e.g. https://inference.do-ai.run/v1
});
const res = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "kimi-k3",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "..." }],
  response_format: { type: "json_object" }, // for the parser step
});
```

Streaming isn't needed for our flow — we return the full ranked list once ranking finishes.

The DO console page you're looking at almost certainly has a **cURL** or **Node.js** tab next to the `Pydo` tab you screenshot'd. Can you switch to one of those and paste it? That will reveal the exact base URL (something like `https://inference.do-ai.run/v1/chat/completions`).

# Construction Matchmaker — Trial Project Plan

## Context

Build a crew-matching micro-app as a 4-hour timed trial for Lemonlight. A general contractor pastes a one-sentence project description ("need a licensed electrician in Austin tomorrow for a kitchen rewire") and the app returns ranked crew matches from an internal database of 10,000 tradespeople, with a one-line rationale per match explaining why they fit.

The build will be demoed and torn into on a 1-hour interview call. Every technical choice must be defensible on latency, cost, and how it would evolve past MVP. Explicitly out of scope: auth, analytics, cost optimization, date/time availability, and any page beyond the search view — but each will be probed verbally, so talking points are prepped in this plan.

Working directory is empty (`F:\web-clients\lemonlight` — only `.gitignore` + empty `server/`, `client/`, `shared/` created so far). This is a greenfield project.

## Stack

- **Frontend:** Vite + React (single page, no state library, plain `fetch`)
- **Backend:** Node 20 + Express + Mongoose
- **DB:** MongoDB Atlas M0 (free tier) with Atlas Search index for BM25 text ranking + 2dsphere geo index
- **LLM:** Ollama Cloud, OpenAI-compatible, via the `openai` Node SDK pointed at the Ollama base URL. Model configurable via `OLLAMA_MODEL` env var (default `gpt-oss:20b`)
- **Seed:** `@faker-js/faker` + curated construction role list + weighted US city coords
- **Dev orchestration:** `concurrently` at the root to run server + client together

## Repo layout

```
F:\web-clients\lemonlight\
├── .env                  # user-populated (gitignored)
├── .env.example          # template
├── .gitignore            # done
├── package.json          # root, dev scripts + concurrently
├── shared/
│   ├── roles.js          # 25 construction roles + skill vocab
│   └── cities.js         # ~200 US cities with lat/lng + weight
├── server/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── index.js      # Express bootstrap
│   │   ├── db.js         # Mongo connection
│   │   ├── llm.js        # OpenAI SDK factory pointed at Ollama
│   │   ├── models/
│   │   │   ├── Crew.js
│   │   │   └── SearchLog.js
│   │   └── routes/
│   │       └── search.js # POST /api/search
│   └── scripts/
│       ├── smoke.js      # verify Mongo + LLM connectivity
│       └── seed.js       # generate 10,000 crew records
└── client/
    ├── package.json
    ├── vite.config.js
    ├── index.html
    └── src/
        ├── main.jsx
        ├── App.jsx       # entire UI
        └── index.css
```

## Data model

### `Crew`
```
name          string
roles         [string]        // e.g. ["carpenter", "framer"]
skills        [string]        // e.g. ["hardwood floors", "cabinet install"]
yearsExperience  number
city          string
state         string
location      { type: "Point", coordinates: [lng, lat] }   // 2dsphere index
hourlyRate    number
rating        number           // 1.0 – 5.0
certifications [string]        // e.g. ["OSHA 30", "EPA Lead-Safe"]
bookingStatus  enum            // "available" | "booked" | "unavailable"
bio           string           // 1–2 sentence blurb (goes into Atlas Search)
```

**Indexes:**
- `2dsphere` on `location`
- Atlas Search index on `roles`, `skills`, `certifications`, `bio` (BM25)
- Plain index on `bookingStatus` (for the availability filter)

### `SearchLog`
```
query           string
parsedFilters   object    // structured JSON returned by LLM
resultIds       [ObjectId]
topRationales   [string]
latencyMs       number
createdAt       Date      // default: now
```
Inserted fire-and-forget (no `await`) so it never blocks the response. This is the substrate the brief calls out for "future training and analysis."

## Request flow — `POST /api/search`

Input: `{ description: string }`

1. **Parse** — Call Ollama with a system prompt telling it to extract structured filters from the sentence. Use `response_format: { type: "json_object" }` and a short JSON schema in the prompt. Output shape:
   ```
   { roles: [string], location: { city, state } | null, radiusMi: number,
     requiredSkills: [string], urgencyDays: number, projectType: string }
   ```
2. **Rank** — Mongo aggregation pipeline:
   ```
   $search (BM25 over roles+skills+bio)
     → $match { bookingStatus: "available" }
     → $geoNear (if location resolved) — else skip
     → $addFields { matchScore: 0.5*searchScore + 0.3*geoScore + 0.2*(rating/5) }
     → $sort { matchScore: -1 }
     → $limit 10
   ```
3. **Rationale** — Single batched Ollama call: pass the parsed filters + the 10 top records, ask for one sentence per crew member explaining fit. One round-trip, not ten.
4. **Log** — Fire-and-forget `SearchLog.create({...})`. No await.
5. **Respond** — `{ results: [{...crew, matchScore, rationale}], parsedFilters, latencyMs }`

**Target:** p95 < 2s. If Ollama rationale latency exceeds budget on the live demo, fall back to a template rationale rendered from the crew fields ("Master carpenter, 12 yrs, 8 mi from job site, available now").

## Seed script (10,000 records)

- **Roles (25, weighted realistically):** carpenter, framer, electrician (residential/commercial), plumber, roofer, HVAC tech, drywall installer, painter, tile setter, mason, concrete finisher, flooring installer, insulation installer, siding installer, foundation specialist, excavator operator, general laborer, project supervisor, welder, glazier, landscaper, cabinet maker, demolition, waterproofing.
- **Cities:** ~200 US cities with real lat/lng, weighted by metro population (denser matches in Houston/Phoenix/Dallas/etc.).
- **Availability distribution:** 70% available, 20% booked, 10% unavailable.
- **Experience:** 1–35 yrs, skewed to 5–15.
- **Rating:** 1.0–5.0, skewed to 3.8–4.6.
- **Runs in one command:** `npm run seed` — batched `insertMany` of 1,000 at a time.
- After seed, script creates Atlas Search index programmatically (or prints manual step if API scope is too painful).

## React UI (one page)

- Header: "Construction Matchmaker"
- `<textarea>` + `<button>Find Crew</button>`
- Loading skeletons while request is in flight
- Results: responsive card grid. Each card:
  - Name (bold)
  - Role badges (chips)
  - City + distance (if location resolved)
  - Star rating
  - Availability chip (green "Available")
  - Rationale in italic, one line
- Collapsible **"Parsed as"** panel showing the LLM's structured extraction — this is the "look under the hood" moment on the demo call.
- Empty state (no matches), error state, and slow-network state all handled.

## 4-hour build budget

| Block | Time |
|---|---|
| Root scaffold, `.env.example`, server `package.json`, Vite client, `npm install` | 30 min |
| `Crew` + `SearchLog` models, seed script, run seed against Atlas | 45 min |
| `/api/search` (parse → aggregation → rationale → log) | 75 min |
| React UI + wire up | 60 min |
| Polish, error/empty states, demo dry-run, prep talking points | 30 min |

## Interview-prep talking points (out-of-scope questions)

- **Auth:** JWT with role claim (contractor vs admin); `ownerOrgId` on Crew for multi-tenant.
- **Analytics:** `SearchLog` is already the substrate — pipe to warehouse (BigQuery), dashboards on match-accept rate, no-result rate, geographic supply gaps.
- **Cost:** Cache parsed filters by sentence hash (SHA-256); LLM only re-invoked on cache miss. Drop LLM rationale for templates if scale hurts. Pre-embed crew and switch to vector search at 1M+ records.
- **Date/time availability:** Booking calendar collection per crew, indexed by day. Query becomes `availabilityWindow ∩ projectWindow`.
- **Why not vector search now:** 10k records + structured skill vocabulary means BM25 + geo wins on latency, cost, and *explainability* (we can point at exactly which term matched). Vectors help when queries get fuzzy ("someone good with historic homes") — I'd add them as a second scoring signal, not a replacement.
- **What if Ollama is down:** Circuit breaker → fall back to keyword parser (regex against role dictionary) and template rationale. Search still works, just with less nuance.

## Critical files (to be created)

- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\package.json` — root, `dev`/`seed`/`smoke` scripts
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\.env.example` — MONGODB_URI, OLLAMA_API_KEY, OLLAMA_BASE_URL, OLLAMA_MODEL, PORT
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\package.json` — express, mongoose, openai, cors, @faker-js/faker
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\src\index.js` — Express bootstrap, `/api/health`, mounts search route
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\src\db.js` — Mongoose connect
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\src\llm.js` — OpenAI SDK factory (baseURL from env)
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\src\models\Crew.js`
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\src\models\SearchLog.js`
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\src\routes\search.js` — the main endpoint
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\scripts\smoke.js` — Mongo + LLM sanity check
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\server\scripts\seed.js` — 10k records + Atlas Search index setup
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\shared\roles.js` — role vocabulary
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\shared\cities.js` — ~200 US cities with coords
- `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\client\*` — Vite scaffold + `App.jsx`

## Verification (end-to-end)

1. User fills `F:\web-clients\lemonlight\.env` with real values.
2. `npm run install:all` — installs root + server + client deps.
3. `npm run smoke` — expects: `mongo connected: matchmaker` and `model=... says: pong`. Both must pass before proceeding.
4. `npm run seed` — expects: `seeded 10000 crew records` in <60s.
5. `npm run dev` — server on `:3001`, client on `:5173`.
6. Open http://localhost:5173, enter a test description ("Need a licensed electrician in Austin for a kitchen rewire tomorrow"), verify:
   - Returns 10 results within ~2s
   - Top result is an electrician (or related) in or near Austin, marked Available
   - "Parsed as" panel shows `roles: ["electrician"], location: {city: "Austin", state: "TX"}, urgencyDays: 1`
   - Each result has a rationale that references the sentence
7. Query MongoDB Atlas: `db.searchlogs.find().sort({createdAt:-1}).limit(1)` — verify the query was logged with parsedFilters, resultIds, latencyMs.
8. Test three edge cases before the call: (a) no location mentioned, (b) rare specialty ("stone mason for a historic chimney restoration"), (c) location with no available crew.

## Open items (need from user)

resultIds       [ObjectId]

Explicitly out of scope: auth, analytics, cost optimization, date/time availability, and any page beyond the search view — but each will be probed verbally, so talking points are prepped in this plan.

Working directory is empty (`F:\web-clients\lemonlight` — only `.gitignore` + empty `server/`, `client/`, `shared/` created so far). This is a greenfield project.

## Stack

- **Frontend:** Vite + React (single page, no state library, plain `fetch`)
- **Backend:** Node 20 + Express + Mongoose
- **DB:** MongoDB Atlas M0 (free tier) with Atlas Search index for BM25 text ranking + 2dsphere geo index
- **LLM:** Ollama Cloud, OpenAI-compatible, via the `openai` Node SDK pointed at the Ollama base URL. Model configurable via `OLLAMA_MODEL` env var (default `gpt-oss:20b`)

├── .env.example          # template

├── server/

│   │   ├── db.js         # Mongo connection
│   │   ├── llm.js        # OpenAI SDK factory pointed at Ollama
│   │   ├── models/
│   │   │   ├── Crew.js
│   │   │   └── SearchLog.js

## Data model

### `Crew`
```
name          string
roles         [string]        // e.g. ["carpenter", "framer"]
skills        [string]        // e.g. ["hardwood floors", "cabinet install"]
yearsExperience  number
city          string
state         string
location      { type: "Point", coordinates: [lng, lat] }   // 2dsphere index
hourlyRate    number
rating        number           // 1.0 – 5.0
certifications [string]        // e.g. ["OSHA 30", "EPA Lead-Safe"]
bookingStatus  enum            // "available" | "booked" | "unavailable"
bio           string           // 1–2 sentence blurb (goes into Atlas Search)
```

**Indexes:**
- `2dsphere` on `location`
- Atlas Search index on `roles`, `skills`, `certifications`, `bio` (BM25)
- Plain index on `bookingStatus` (for the availability filter)

### `SearchLog`
```
query           string
parsedFilters   object    // structured JSON returned by LLM
resultIds       [ObjectId]
topRationales   [string]
latencyMs       number
createdAt       Date      // default: now
```
Inserted fire-and-forget (no `await`) so it never blocks the response. This is the substrate the brief calls out for "future training and analysis."

## Request flow — `POST /api/search`

Input: `{ description: string }`

1. **Parse** — Call Ollama with a system prompt telling it to extract structured filters from the sentence. Use `response_format: { type: "json_object" }` and a short JSON schema in the prompt. Output shape:
   ```
   { roles: [string], location: { city, state } | null, radiusMi: number,
     requiredSkills: [string], urgencyDays: number, projectType: string }
   ```
2. **Rank** — Mongo aggregation pipeline:
   ```
   $search (BM25 over roles+skills+bio)
     → $match { bookingStatus: "available" }
     → $geoNear (if location resolved) — else skip
     → $addFields { matchScore: 0.5*searchScore + 0.3*geoScore + 0.2*(rating/5) }
     → $sort { matchScore: -1 }
     → $limit 10
   ```
3. **Rationale** — Single batched Ollama call: pass the parsed filters + the 10 top records, ask for one sentence per crew member explaining fit. One round-trip, not ten.
4. **Log** — Fire-and-forget `SearchLog.create({...})`. No await.
5. **Respond** — `{ results: [{...crew, matchScore, rationale}], parsedFilters, latencyMs }`

**Target:** p95 < 2s. If Ollama rationale latency exceeds budget on the live demo, fall back to a template rationale rendered from the crew fields ("Master carpenter, 12 yrs, 8 mi from job site, available now").

## Seed script (10,000 records)

- **Roles (25, weighted realistically):** carpenter, framer, electrician (residential/commercial), plumber, roofer, HVAC tech, drywall installer, painter, tile setter, mason, concrete finisher, flooring installer, insulation installer, siding installer, foundation specialist, excavator operator, general laborer, project supervisor, welder, glazier, landscaper, cabinet maker, demolition, waterproofing.
- **Cities:** ~200 US cities with real lat/lng, weighted by metro population (denser matches in Houston/Phoenix/Dallas/etc.).
- **Availability distribution:** 70% available, 20% booked, 10% unavailable.
- **Experience:** 1–35 yrs, skewed to 5–15.
- **Rating:** 1.0–5.0, skewed to 3.8–4.6.
- **Runs in one command:** `npm run seed` — batched `insertMany` of 1,000 at a time.
- After seed, script creates Atlas Search index programmatically (or prints manual step if API scope is too painful).

## React UI (one page)

- Header: "Construction Matchmaker"
- `<textarea>` + `<button>Find Crew</button>`
- Loading skeletons while request is in flight
- Results: responsive card grid. Each card:
  - Name (bold)
  - Role badges (chips)
  - City + distance (if location resolved)
  - Star rating
  - Availability chip (green "Available")
  - Rationale in italic, one line
- Collapsible **"Parsed as"** panel showing the LLM's structured extraction — this is the "look under the hood" moment on the demo call.

# System overview

## One-line summary

A general contractor types a one-sentence project description; the app returns
10 ranked matches from a 10,000-person crew database, each annotated with a
one-line rationale for why they fit.

## Component diagram

```
 ┌──────────────────┐        POST /api/search        ┌──────────────────────┐
 │  React SPA       │ ─────────────────────────────▶ │  Express API         │
 │  (Vite, :5173)   │ ◀───────────────────────────── │  (Node 20, :3001)    │
 └──────────────────┘        { results, ... }        └──────────┬───────────┘
                                                                │
                          ┌─────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
                          │                                     │                     │
                          ▼                                     ▼                     ▼
                 ┌─────────────────┐               ┌────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
                 │ Groq            │               │ MongoDB Atlas M0   │   │ MongoDB Atlas M0 │
                 │ (openai/        │               │  ─ crew            │   │  ─ searchlogs    │
                 │  gpt-oss-120b)  │               │    (Atlas Search   │   │    (append-only) │
                 │                 │               │     + 2dsphere)    │   │                  │
                 └─────────────────┘               └────────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘
```

## Request lifecycle (compressed)

1. User types description → clicks Find Crew
2. `POST /api/search { description }`
3. Server calls Groq (`gpt-oss-120b`) with JSON-mode prompt → structured filters
4. Server runs one Mongo aggregation: Atlas Search + `$match` availability + `$geoNear` + score blend + `$limit 10`
5. Server calls Groq once with the top 10 records → gets 10 rationale strings back
6. Server fires `SearchLog.create(...)` (no await) to persist the query for training
7. Server returns `{ results, parsedFilters, latencyMs }`
8. React renders result cards + collapsible "Parsed as" panel

## Tech stack rationale

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Frontend | Vite + React, no state library | 4-hour budget. `useState` + `fetch` covers the single page. |
| Backend | Node 20 + Express + Mongoose | Familiar, minimal boilerplate. `--env-file` avoids a `dotenv` dependency. |
| Database | MongoDB Atlas M0 (free) | Native Atlas Search (BM25) + `$geoNear` in one pipeline stage. No sidecar search service. |
| LLM | Groq · `openai/gpt-oss-120b` | Groq's throughput on gpt-oss-120b is sub-second for our prompt sizes — critical for keeping p95 < 2s across two LLM hops. OpenAI-compatible so we use the `openai` npm SDK. |
| Seed | `@faker-js/faker` + curated vocabularies | Faker for names/dates; hand-curated role + city lists so the search results actually make sense. |

## Latency budget

Target: **p95 < 2s** end-to-end.

| Stage | Budget |
|---|---|
| Network (client → server) | 50 ms |
| Groq parse call | 400 ms |
| Mongo aggregation | 200 ms |
| Groq rationale call (batched, all 10 at once) | 800 ms |
| Serialize + network back | 50 ms |
| **Total** | **~1.5 s** |

`SearchLog.create` is fire-and-forget — it never adds to the response path.

## What's deliberately not in the diagram

Auth, analytics pipelines, availability/calendaring, admin CRUD, and vector
search — all of these are covered as "how would you approach it" in
[`future-work.md`](./future-work.md).

# Data model

Two collections. `crew` is the searchable roster; `searchlogs` is the
append-only record of what contractors asked for and what came back.

## `crew`

```
{
  _id            ObjectId
  name           string           // "Marcus Alvarez"
  roles          [string]         // ["carpenter", "framer"]  — canonical keys from shared/roles.js
  skills         [string]         // ["hardwood floors", "cabinet install"]
  yearsExperience  number         // 1–35
  city           string           // "Austin"
  state          string           // "TX"
  location       {                // GeoJSON Point — 2dsphere index
    type: "Point",
    coordinates: [lng, lat]
  }
  hourlyRate     number           // USD
  rating         number           // 1.0–5.0, one decimal
  certifications [string]         // ["OSHA 30", "EPA Lead-Safe"]
  bookingStatus  enum             // "available" | "booked" | "unavailable"
  bio            string           // 1–2 sentences. Fed into Atlas Search text index.
  createdAt      Date
  updatedAt      Date
}
```

### Why each field

- **`roles` (array, not single value):** Real tradespeople carry multiple
  hats. A carpenter who also frames. A supervisor who welds. Modeling this as
  an array is the difference between "top match" and "best match."
- **`skills`:** More granular than roles. Roles are the coarse filter; skills
  are what the LLM's parsed `requiredSkills` actually match against in Atlas
  Search.
- **`location` as GeoJSON Point:** required by `$geoNear`. `city`/`state` are
  denormalized for display and easy `_ne "location resolved"_` handling.
- **`bio`:** Free-text field that gives BM25 something to score against for
  fuzzy queries like "someone good with historic homes." Generated by the
  seeder from role + skills + a few templated phrases.

# Search flow — end-to-end

What happens when a contractor clicks "Find Crew."

## 1. Client sends request

```
POST /api/search
Content-Type: application/json

{ "description": "Need a licensed electrician in Austin for a kitchen rewire tomorrow" }
```

Client shows loading skeletons immediately; timeout at 8s.

## 2. Server: parse the sentence into structured filters

Call Groq with `openai/gpt-oss-120b` in JSON mode.

**System prompt** (paraphrased — actual text lives in `server/src/routes/search.js`):

> You are a query parser for a construction crew matchmaker. Extract structured
> filters from a natural-language project description. Return valid JSON matching
> the schema below. Use only role keys from this vocabulary: `[carpenter,
> electrician, plumber, ...]`. If a field is not mentioned, return an empty
> array, `null`, or a sensible default.

**Schema returned:**

```json
{
  "roles": ["electrician"],
  "requiredSkills": ["kitchen rewire"],
  "location": { "city": "Austin", "state": "TX" },
  "radiusMi": 50,
  "urgencyDays": 1,
  "projectType": "residential"
}
```

Two guardrails:
- **JSON mode:** `response_format: { type: "json_object" }` on the Groq call
  so we never have to parse markdown fences.
- **Role vocabulary is passed in the prompt** — the LLM can only pick from
  the 25 canonical role keys, so downstream Mongo matches don't misfire on
  hallucinated categories.

If parsing throws (JSON invalid, or LLM 5xx), fall back to a regex parser
that scans the description against the aliases in `shared/roles.js` and
returns a minimal filter object. Search still works, just with less nuance.

## 3. Server: rank candidates via Mongo aggregation

One pipeline. Runs against the `crew` collection.

```js
[
  {
    $search: {
      index: "crew_default",
      compound: {
        should: [
          { text: { query: filters.roles,          path: "roles",          score: { boost: { value: 5 } } } },
          { text: { query: filters.requiredSkills, path: "skills",         score: { boost: { value: 3 } } } },
          { text: { query: filters.requiredSkills, path: "bio",            score: { boost: { value: 1 } } } },
        ],
      },
    },
  },
  { $match: { bookingStatus: "available" } },

  // Only if location resolved:
  { $geoNear: { near: filters.location.point, distanceField: "distanceMeters", spherical: true, maxDistance: filters.radiusMi * 1609 } },

  { $addFields: {
      searchScore: { $meta: "searchScore" },
      geoScore: { $cond: [ { $ifNull: ["$distanceMeters", false] },
                            { $subtract: [1, { $divide: ["$distanceMeters", filters.radiusMi * 1609] }] },
                            0.5 ] },
      matchScore: { $add: [
        { $multiply: [{ $meta: "searchScore" }, 0.5] },
        { $multiply: ["$geoScore", 0.3] },
        { $multiply: [{ $divide: ["$rating", 5] }, 0.2] },
      ] },
    },
  },
  { $sort: { matchScore: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 },
  { $project: { bio: 1, name: 1, roles: 1, skills: 1, city: 1, state: 1,
                 rating: 1, hourlyRate: 1, yearsExperience: 1, certifications: 1,
                 bookingStatus: 1, distanceMeters: 1, matchScore: 1 } },
]
```

Note: `$search` **must** be the first stage. `$geoNear` cannot follow `$search`
directly in the same pipeline in all Mongo versions — this is a known
constraint. Workaround if we hit it: do search-then-manual-distance-in-JS for
the top 50 candidates, then sort. TBD during build.

## 4. Server: batched rationale generation

Single Groq call with the original description + the 10 top records.

**Prompt:**

> The contractor's request: `"{description}"`.
>
> For each crew member below, write one short sentence explaining why they're
> a fit for this specific request. Reference concrete details from their
> record (role, location relative to the job, standout skills, experience).
> Return a JSON object: `{ "rationales": ["...", "...", ...] }` in the same
> order as the crew list.
>
> Crew: `[{ name, roles, skills, city, state, yearsExperience, distanceMi, certifications }, ...]`

Ten rationales in one round-trip beats ten separate calls on both latency and
cost. Groq's JSON mode ensures parseable output.

If this call fails, fall back to a template rationale per crew member:

> `"${topRole}, ${yearsExperience} yrs experience, ${distanceMi} mi from
> ${city} — ${bookingStatus}."`

## 5. Server: fire-and-forget log

```js
SearchLog.create({
  query: description,
  parsedFilters: filters,
  resultIds: results.map(r => r._id),
  topRationales: rationales,
  latencyMs: Date.now() - t0,
}).catch(err => console.error("searchlog write failed:", err));
```

No `await`. Runs in the background. Response goes out first.

## 6. Server: respond

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "_id": "...",
      "name": "Marcus Alvarez",
      "roles": ["electrician"],
      "skills": ["kitchen rewire", "panel upgrades"],
      "city": "Austin",
      "state": "TX",
      "yearsExperience": 12,
      "rating": 4.7,
      "hourlyRate": 85,
      "certifications": ["OSHA 30", "Journeyman License"],
      "bookingStatus": "available",
      "distanceMi": 3.4,
      "matchScore": 0.87,
      "rationale": "Local Austin electrician with 12 years and kitchen rewire experience — 3 miles from the job and available now."
    }
    // ... 9 more
  ],
  "parsedFilters": { "roles": ["electrician"], "location": {...}, ... },
  "latencyMs": 1230
}
```

## Failure modes

| What breaks | What happens |
|---|---|
| Groq parse call errors | Regex fallback parser runs. `parsedFilters._fallback: true` set. |
| Mongo returns 0 results | Response is `{ results: [], parsedFilters, latencyMs }`. Client shows empty state with the parsed filters (so contractor can see we understood, just don't have anyone). |
| Groq rationale call errors | Template rationales substituted. Response still returns 10 crew. |
| Mongo down | 503 to client. |
| Search takes > 8s | Client times out, shows error. Server keeps running (may still write log). |

# LLM integration

## Provider: Groq

- **Base URL:** `https://api.groq.com/openai/v1`
- **Auth:** `Authorization: Bearer $GROQ_API_KEY`
- **Model:** `openai/gpt-oss-120b` (configurable via `GROQ_MODEL`)
- **SDK:** `openai` npm package pointed at Groq's OpenAI-compatible endpoint

### Why Groq

- **Throughput.** Groq's LPU inference on gpt-oss-120b is sub-second for our
  prompt sizes. We're doing two LLM hops per search (parse + rationale) and
  still need to stay under a 2s p95 — this doesn't work on most other hosted
  providers without heroic engineering.
- **OpenAI-compatible.** Zero SDK lock-in. If we need to swap models, we
  change one env var. If we need to swap providers entirely, we change one
  more.
- **gpt-oss-120b is a strong open model.** JSON mode is well-supported. It
  handles the parsing task with a short prompt and no fine-tuning.

### Client setup

Single factory in `server/src/llm.js`:

```js
import OpenAI from "openai";

let client;
export function getLLM() {
  if (client) return client;
  const apiKey = process.env.GROQ_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("GROQ_API_KEY not set");
  const baseURL = process.env.GROQ_BASE_URL || "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1";
  client = new OpenAI({ apiKey, baseURL });
  return client;
}

export const MODEL = process.env.GROQ_MODEL || "openai/gpt-oss-120b";
```

Cached at module scope so we don't re-instantiate per request.

## Prompts

Both prompts live in `server/src/routes/search.js` so the search flow is
readable end-to-end in a single file. If a third LLM use appears, extract
them to `server/src/prompts/`.

### Parser prompt

**Role: system**

```
You extract structured filters from a natural-language construction project
description written by a general contractor.

Return valid JSON matching this schema exactly:

{
  "roles": string[],           // pick 0+ keys from the ROLES vocabulary below. lowercase, exact match.
  "requiredSkills": string[],  // short skill phrases mentioned or implied (e.g. "kitchen rewire", "shingle replacement")
  "location": { "city": string, "state": string } | null,
  "radiusMi": number,          // reasonable default 50; smaller for urgent same-day requests
  "urgencyDays": number,       // 0 = today, 1 = tomorrow, 7 = this week, 30 = anytime
  "projectType": string        // "residential" | "commercial" | "mixed"
}

ROLES vocabulary: [carpenter, electrician, plumber, roofer, hvac, drywall,
painter, tile, mason, concrete, flooring, insulation, siding, foundation,
excavator, laborer, supervisor, welder, glazier, landscaper, cabinet,
demolition, waterproofing, solar, gutter]

Rules:
- Return ONLY the JSON. No prose, no markdown fences.
- If a role isn't explicitly named but is implied by the task (e.g.
  "rewire" → electrician, "reshingle" → roofer), include the implied role.
- If location is ambiguous or missing, set to null.
- If urgency is unclear, default urgencyDays to 7.
```

**Role: user**

```
{description}
```

**Call config:**

```js
llm.chat.completions.create({
  model: MODEL,
  messages: [{ role: "system", content: PARSER_SYSTEM }, { role: "user", content: description }],
  response_format: { type: "json_object" },
  max_tokens: 300,
  temperature: 0.1,
});
```

Low temperature — this is extraction, not generation.

### Rationale prompt

**Role: system**

```
You explain why each of these crew members is a strong fit for the
contractor's request. One sentence per crew, referencing concrete details
(role, location relative to job, standout skill, experience). Return valid
JSON: { "rationales": string[] } — same order as the input crew list.

Be specific and honest. If a crew member is a weaker fit than the others,
lead with what they DO bring (e.g. availability, distance) rather than
overselling role alignment.
```

**Role: user**

```
Request: "{description}"
Parsed as: {parsedFilters as JSON}

Crew (in ranked order):
[
  { "name": "...", "roles": [...], "skills": [...], "city": "...", "state": "...",
    "yearsExperience": ..., "distanceMi": ..., "certifications": [...] },
  ...
]
```

**Call config:**

```js
llm.chat.completions.create({
  model: MODEL,
  messages: [{ role: "system", content: RATIONALE_SYSTEM }, { role: "user", content: userPayload }],
  response_format: { type: "json_object" },
  max_tokens: 800,
  temperature: 0.4,
});
```

Slightly higher temperature — a bit of variety in phrasing is good UX.
Bounded at 800 tokens so a runaway response can't blow the latency budget.

## Fallbacks

Both LLM calls are wrapped in try/catch. Any failure trips the fallback path:

- **Parser fallback:** regex the description against role aliases from
  `shared/roles.js`. Extract location by looking for `"in <TitleCase>"`
  patterns and cross-referencing `shared/cities.js`. Set `_fallback: true`
  on the parsed filter object so the client "Parsed as" panel can indicate
  we're in degraded mode.

- **Rationale fallback:** for each crew, emit a template string:

  ```
  ${primaryRole}, ${yearsExperience} yrs, ${city} ${state} — ${bookingStatus}.
  ```

The search endpoint therefore never hard-fails on LLM issues. Worst case
the contractor still gets 10 candidates with terse rationales.

## Cost & rate limits

Not addressed at MVP (out of scope per brief), but see
[`future-work.md`](./future-work.md) for the plan: SHA-256 cache on
`description → parsedFilters`, drop rationale LLM at high scale in favor
of templates, and switch to a smaller model for the parse step if latency
allows.

import OpenAI from "openai";

let client;
export function getLLM() {
  if (client) return client;
  const apiKey = process.env.GROQ_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("GROQ_API_KEY not set");
  const baseURL = process.env.GROQ_BASE_URL || "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1";
  client = new OpenAI({ apiKey, baseURL });
  return client;
}

export const MODEL = process.env.GROQ_MODEL || "openai/gpt-oss-120b";
```

Cached at module scope so we don't re-instantiate per request.

## Prompts

Both prompts live in `server/src/routes/search.js` so the search flow is
readable end-to-end in a single file. If a third LLM use appears, extract
them to `server/src/prompts/`.

### Parser prompt

**Role: system**

```
You extract structured filters from a natural-language construction project
description written by a general contractor.

Return valid JSON matching this schema exactly:

{
  "roles": string[],           // pick 0+ keys from the ROLES vocabulary below. lowercase, exact match.
  "requiredSkills": string[],  // short skill phrases mentioned or implied (e.g. "kitchen rewire", "shingle replacement")
  "location": { "city": string, "state": string } | null,
  "radiusMi": number,          // reasonable default 50; smaller for urgent same-day requests
  "urgencyDays": number,       // 0 = today, 1 = tomorrow, 7 = this week, 30 = anytime
  "projectType": string        // "residential" | "commercial" | "mixed"
}

ROLES vocabulary: [carpenter, electrician, plumber, roofer, hvac, drywall,
painter, tile, mason, concrete, flooring, insulation, siding, foundation,
excavator, laborer, supervisor, welder, glazier, landscaper, cabinet,
demolition, waterproofing, solar, gutter]

Rules:
- Return ONLY the JSON. No prose, no markdown fences.
- If a role isn't explicitly named but is implied by the task (e.g.
  "rewire" → electrician, "reshingle" → roofer), include the implied role.
- If location is ambiguous or missing, set to null.
- If urgency is unclear, default urgencyDays to 7.
```

**Role: user**

```
{description}
```

**Call config:**

```js
llm.chat.completions.create({
  model: MODEL,
  messages: [{ role: "system", content: PARSER_SYSTEM }, { role: "user", content: description }],
  response_format: { type: "json_object" },
  max_tokens: 300,
  temperature: 0.1,
});
```

Low temperature — this is extraction, not generation.

### Rationale prompt

**Role: system**

```
You explain why each of these crew members is a strong fit for the
contractor's request. One sentence per crew, referencing concrete details
(role, location relative to job, standout skill, experience). Return valid
JSON: { "rationales": string[] } — same order as the input crew list.

Be specific and honest. If a crew member is a weaker fit than the others,
lead with what they DO bring (e.g. availability, distance) rather than
overselling role alignment.
```

**Role: user**

```
Request: "{description}"
Parsed as: {parsedFilters as JSON}

Crew (in ranked order):
[
  { "name": "...", "roles": [...], "skills": [...], "city": "...", "state": "...",
    "yearsExperience": ..., "distanceMi": ..., "certifications": [...] },
  ...
]
```

**Call config:**

```js
llm.chat.completions.create({
  model: MODEL,
  messages: [{ role: "system", content: RATIONALE_SYSTEM }, { role: "user", content: userPayload }],
  response_format: { type: "json_object" },
  max_tokens: 800,
  temperature: 0.4,
});
```

Slightly higher temperature — a bit of variety in phrasing is good UX.
Bounded at 800 tokens so a runaway response can't blow the latency budget.

## Fallbacks

Both LLM calls are wrapped in try/catch. Any failure trips the fallback path:

- **Parser fallback:** regex the description against role aliases from
  `shared/roles.js`. Extract location by looking for `"in <TitleCase>"`
  patterns and cross-referencing `shared/cities.js`. Set `_fallback: true`
  on the parsed filter object so the client "Parsed as" panel can indicate
  we're in degraded mode.

- **Rationale fallback:** for each crew, emit a template string:

  ```
  ${primaryRole}, ${yearsExperience} yrs, ${city} ${state} — ${bookingStatus}.
  ```

The search endpoint therefore never hard-fails on LLM issues. Worst case
the contractor still gets 10 candidates with terse rationales.

## Cost & rate limits

Not addressed at MVP (out of scope per brief), but see
[`future-work.md`](./future-work.md) for the plan: SHA-256 cache on
`description → parsedFilters`, drop rationale LLM at high scale in favor
of templates, and switch to a smaller model for the parse step if latency
allows.

# Seeding — 10,000 crew records

The brief mandates 10k people covering the full range of construction roles
across the entire United States. The distribution matters — a uniform random
seed produces a database where every search returns implausible matches.

## Script

`server/scripts/seed.js` — run with `npm run seed` from repo root.

Behavior:
1. Connect to Atlas via `MONGODB_URI`.
2. Drop the `crew` collection (idempotent re-seeds).
3. Generate 10,000 records in memory using `@faker-js/faker` + curated
   vocabularies from `shared/roles.js` and `shared/cities.js`.
4. `insertMany` in batches of 1,000.
5. Ensure the `2dsphere` index on `location` and the plain index on
   `bookingStatus`.
6. Attempt to create the Atlas Search index `crew_default` via the Atlas
   Admin API (if `ATLAS_PUBLIC_KEY`/`ATLAS_PRIVATE_KEY` env vars are set).
   Otherwise print the definition JSON and the console URL so it can be
   created in one click.

## Distributions

### Role coverage

Weighted by real-world construction workforce composition (roughly):

| Role bucket | Weight | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| carpenter / framer | 15 | most common trade |
| electrician | 12 | high demand, high pay |
| plumber | 10 | universal need |
| general laborer | 10 | day-laborer bucket the brief calls out |
| painter | 8 | |
| drywall | 7 | |
| hvac | 7 | |
| roofer | 6 | |
| flooring | 5 | |
| mason, concrete, tile | 4 each | |
| supervisor | 4 | |
| specialty (welder, glazier, cabinet, waterproofing, foundation, siding, insulation, demolition, solar, gutter, landscaper, excavator) | 1–3 each | |

Roughly 20% of crew get a **second role** so we can model tradespeople with
overlapping skills (a carpenter who also does trim; a supervisor who welds).

### Geographic distribution

`shared/cities.js` contains ~100 US cities each tagged with an approximate
metro-population weight. The seeder samples a city weighted by that number,
then jitters the lat/lng by up to ±0.3° so the map isn't dotted with
identical points on top of city centers.

Result: dense clusters around Houston, Phoenix, Dallas, LA, NYC, Chicago;
sparser but real coverage of Fargo, Boise, Chattanooga, Anchorage.

### Availability

| Status | Share |
|---|---|
| `available` | 70% |
| `booked` | 20% |
| `unavailable` | 10% |

Ensures the availability filter matters (a naive query would silently drop
30% of the roster) but doesn't starve the search of results.

### Experience & rating

- `yearsExperience`: 1–35, skewed toward 5–15 (Faker `.number.int()` with a
  bell-shaped custom sampler).
- `rating`: 1.0–5.0, skewed toward 3.8–4.6. Very low ratings are rare in
  reality — most tradespeople who stay in business have decent reputations.

### Skills

Per crew, 3–6 skills sampled from the `SKILL_POOL_BY_ROLE` map for whichever
role(s) they hold. This ensures a "kitchen rewire" query surfaces the
electricians who actually claim that skill, not every electrician.

### Certifications

40% of crew have at least one certification, sampled from the pool in
`shared/roles.js`. Higher for electricians (journeyman/master), roofers
(OSHA 30), and solar installers (NABCEP).

### Bio

Generated by concatenating templated phrases keyed off the crew's roles and
skills, seasoned with a Faker sentence for flavor:

> "Marcus is a residential electrician based in Austin with 12 years on the
> tools. Specializes in kitchen rewires and panel upgrades. Journeyman
> licensed. Reliable and communicates well."

The bio is the free-text field Atlas Search leans on for fuzzy queries.

## Performance

Batched `insertMany` of 1,000 completes the full 10k seed in ~15-30s on a
free M0 tier. Index creation adds a few seconds.

## Determinism

Faker's seed is set to a fixed value at the top of the script. Re-running
`npm run seed` produces the same 10k records (modulo Mongo `_id` values).
This matters for the demo — we want reproducible test queries.

# API contracts

Base URL in development: `http://localhost:3001`

All request/response bodies are `application/json`.

## `GET /api/health`

Liveness probe. Returns immediately with no DB or LLM dependency.

**Response 200:**
```json
{ "ok": true }
```

## `POST /api/search`

The only meaningful endpoint. Takes a natural-language project description,
returns ranked crew matches.

### Request

```json
{
  "description": "Need a licensed electrician in Austin for a kitchen rewire tomorrow"
}
```

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `description` | string | yes | 1–1000 chars. Longer is truncated to 1000 with a warning header. |

### Response 200

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "_id": "6712abc...",
      "name": "Marcus Alvarez",
      "roles": ["electrician"],
      "skills": ["kitchen rewire", "panel upgrades"],
      "yearsExperience": 12,
      "city": "Austin",
      "state": "TX",
      "hourlyRate": 85,
      "rating": 4.7,
      "certifications": ["OSHA 30", "Journeyman License"],
      "bookingStatus": "available",
      "distanceMi": 3.4,
      "matchScore": 0.87,
      "rationale": "Local Austin electrician with 12 years and kitchen rewire experience — 3 miles from the job and available now."
    }
  ],
  "parsedFilters": {
    "roles": ["electrician"],
    "requiredSkills": ["kitchen rewire"],
    "location": { "city": "Austin", "state": "TX" },
    "radiusMi": 50,
    "urgencyDays": 1,
    "projectType": "residential"
  },
  "latencyMs": 1230
}
```

**Field notes:**
- `results` is empty array (not null) when no crew match.
- `distanceMi` is omitted when the query has no location.
- `parsedFilters._fallback` is `true` when the LLM parser errored and the
  regex fallback ran.
- `latencyMs` is server-side wall-clock from request start to response
  serialize. Does not include client network time.

### Response 400 — validation

```json
{ "error": "description must be a non-empty string" }
```

Triggered on: missing `description`, empty string, or non-string type.

### Response 503 — dependency failure

```json
{ "error": "database unavailable" }
```

Triggered when Mongo connection is down. LLM failures do NOT return 503 —
they fall through to the regex parser + template rationale path.

## Not implemented (out of scope)

- `POST /api/crew` — add a new crew member
- `PATCH /api/crew/:id/status` — update booking status
- `GET /api/searchlogs` — retrieve logged queries for analysis
- `POST /api/matches/:searchId/accept` — record which candidate was
  actually hired (feedback signal for future ranking)
- Any auth endpoints

See [`future-work.md`](./future-work.md) for how these would fit in.

# Frontend

A single-page React app served by Vite in dev. No routing, no state library,
no UI framework — plain React with hand-written CSS.

## File layout

```
client/
├── index.html
├── vite.config.js
├── package.json
└── src/
    ├── main.jsx        # Vite entry: mounts <App /> into #root
    ├── App.jsx         # the entire UI
    └── index.css       # all styles
```

## Component structure (all in `App.jsx`)

```
<App>                                             // top-level state: description, results, loading, error, parsedFilters
  <Header />                                       // "Construction Matchmaker" + tagline
  <SearchForm                                      // textarea + Find Crew button
    onSubmit={handleSearch}
    disabled={loading}
  />
  <ParsedPanel filters={parsedFilters} />          // collapsible: shows how the LLM parsed the sentence
  <ResultsSection>
    {loading    && <SkeletonGrid count={6} />}
    {error      && <ErrorBanner message={error} />}
    {empty      && <EmptyState filters={parsedFilters} />}
    {hasResults && results.map(r => <CrewCard key={r._id} crew={r} />)}
  </ResultsSection>
</App>
```

Sub-components are defined as small function components in the same file
(not exported). Threshold to split out into their own files: >100 lines.
We won't hit that in a 4-hour build.

## State

```js
const [description, setDescription] = useState("");
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [error, setError] = useState(null);
const [results, setResults] = useState(null);        // null before first search, [] after empty result
const [parsedFilters, setParsedFilters] = useState(null);
const [latencyMs, setLatencyMs] = useState(null);
```

No context, no reducer — the whole flow is: type → submit → set loading →
fetch → set results. React 18 batching handles the three `setState` calls at
the end without extra ceremony.

## Data fetching

Plain `fetch` inside `handleSearch`:

```js
async function handleSearch(desc) {
  setLoading(true);
  setError(null);
  try {
    const res = await fetch("/api/search", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ description: desc }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error((await res.json()).error || res.statusText);
    const data = await res.json();
    setResults(data.results);
    setParsedFilters(data.parsedFilters);
    setLatencyMs(data.latencyMs);
  } catch (err) {
    setError(err.message);
  } finally {
    setLoading(false);
  }
}
```

Vite proxy in `vite.config.js` forwards `/api/*` to `http://localhost:3001`
so we don't have to think about CORS in dev.

## CrewCard visual

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Marcus Alvarez                              ★ 4.7      │
│  [electrician]                                          │
│                                                         │
│  Austin, TX   ·   3 mi   ·   12 yrs   ·   $85/hr        │
│  OSHA 30 · Journeyman License                           │
│                                                         │
│  ● Available                                            │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│  ⓘ  Local Austin electrician with 12 years and         │
│     kitchen rewire experience — 3 miles from the job   │
│     and available now.                                  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## "Parsed as" panel

Collapsed by default. Expanded reveals the raw `parsedFilters` JSON, pretty-
printed. This is the "look under the hood" moment on the demo call — it lets
the interviewer see exactly how the LLM interpreted the sentence.

## Styling

Hand-written CSS in `index.css`. Custom properties for color/spacing scale,
plain flex/grid for layout, no CSS framework.

Palette:
- Neutral background (`#fafaf9`)
- Card background (`#fff`) with subtle shadow
- Primary accent (a construction-adjacent orange — `#d97706`)
- Success chip green (`#059669`), warning yellow, danger red

Mobile responsive via one `@media (max-width: 720px)` breakpoint that
collapses the card grid to a single column.

## Empty / error / loading states

All three are actually implemented, not TODO'd. Interview trap: if you demo
with a rare query and get 0 results, an unhandled empty state looks like
a bug. Same for a Groq outage. Both have explicit UI.

## Accessibility

Not a demo focus but the basics: semantic elements (`<form>`, `<button>`,
`<label>` for the textarea), keyboard-submittable, sufficient contrast on
chips. No color-only status indicators — the availability chip has both
color and label text.

printed. This is the "look under the hood" moment on the demo call — it lets

plain flex/grid for layout, no CSS framework.

- Neutral background (`#fafaf9`)
- Card background (`#fff`) with subtle shadow
- Primary accent (a construction-adjacent orange — `#d97706`)
- Success chip green (`#059669`), warning yellow, danger red

collapses the card grid to a single column.

a bug. Same for a Groq outage. Both have explicit UI.

# Future work / out-of-scope

The brief explicitly excludes these from the MVP but says "we may ask you how
you'd approach them." Each section below is designed to be answered in
2–3 minutes on the interview call, with a concrete approach and a named
tradeoff.

## Authentication

**Approach:** JWT-based, contractor is the primary principal.

- New `User` collection with `email`, `passwordHash` (argon2id), `role`
  (`contractor` | `admin`), `orgId`.
- New `Org` collection so multiple contractors at the same GC firm share a
  crew rolodex and search history.
- `POST /api/auth/login` issues a JWT with `{ userId, orgId, role, exp }`.
- Middleware on `/api/*` validates the JWT and attaches `req.user`.
- `SearchLog` gains `userId` + `orgId`. `crew` gains an optional `ownerOrgId`
  for private-to-org additions vs. the shared national pool.
- No refresh tokens in v1; 24h JWT is fine for a B2B tool. Add refresh
  when we need SSO.

**Tradeoff:** Roll-your-own vs Clerk/Auth0. Auth0 is faster to production and
gets us MFA/SSO for free. Roll-your-own is cheaper and keeps user data in one
database. For a contractor SaaS I'd probably start with Clerk to avoid the
compliance surface.

## Analytics

**Approach:** `SearchLog` is already the substrate. Layer on a lightweight
ETL to a warehouse.

- Nightly job dumps new `SearchLog` docs to BigQuery (or Snowflake / DuckDB
  Motherduck for cheap starts).
- Metabase or Superset dashboards on top of the warehouse.
- Key metrics to track from day one:
  - **Search volume** by city/state/role — where is demand growing
  - **No-result rate** by role/geo — where is the crew supply thin
  - **Match acceptance rate** (once we add a "book this crew" button and log
    that event) — direct signal of ranker quality
  - **Parser drift** — % of queries where `parsedFilters.roles` is empty or
    all-fallback
  - **Latency percentiles** — track p50/p95/p99 by stage (parse vs. rank vs.
    rationale) to know where to optimize

**Tradeoff:** Warehouse ETL vs. product analytics tool like Mixpanel. Mixpanel
is fantastic for event stream analysis but weaker for joining across search
history + booking outcomes. Since we own the data, warehouse.

## Cost optimization

Two knobs to turn, in this order:

1. **Cache the parser.** SHA-256(description) → parsedFilters, TTL 24h,
   stored in Redis or a Mongo capped collection. Cache hit rate should be
   surprisingly high — contractors reuse phrasings ("licensed electrician,"
   "same-day plumber"). This eliminates the parse Groq call for repeat
   queries.
2. **Drop the rationale LLM call** at high scale. Template rationale from
   the crew record fields is 80% as good and 100% free. Retain the LLM
   rationale for the top 1–2 results only; template for the rest.

Second-order: smaller/cheaper parse model. `gpt-oss-20b` on Groq is
probably sufficient for structured extraction; A/B test parser output
quality against `gpt-oss-120b` before switching.

**Tradeoff:** Caching parser output means we don't retrain the parser
regularly. Fine for now — we can bust cache when we ship a new prompt.

## Date/time availability

**Approach:** New `AvailabilityWindow` collection, indexed by crew + date range.

```
{
  crewId: ObjectId,
  from: Date,
  to: Date,
  status: "available" | "booked" | "off"
}
```

- On each search, compute the query's project window from `urgencyDays` +
  optional user-supplied end date.
- Aggregation adds `$lookup` on `availabilitywindows` filtered to overlap
  the project window, then `$match { availWindow: { $exists: true } }`.

**Tradeoff:** `$lookup` on every search costs. Alternative: denormalize a
`nextAvailableDate` field onto each `crew` record, updated by a nightly job
+ webhook on booking changes. Cheaper reads, staler data. For a real
product I'd start with denormalized + eventual consistency.

## Other pages beyond search

- **Crew detail page** (`/crew/:id`): full profile, portfolio photos, past
  contractor reviews, direct-message button.
- **Booking flow**: click a crew card → confirm dates → notification to
  crew's phone → status flips to `booked`.
- **Contractor dashboard**: past searches, in-progress bookings, favorites.
- **Admin crew management** (for the ops team): CRUD, verify licenses, flag
  duplicates.

All standard CRUD. React Router for client routing, Express routes prefixed
by resource. The important architectural question is where **licensed
verification** goes — probably a separate microservice consuming state
licensing board APIs, since that's a compliance surface.

## Vector search / semantic matching

**When it starts mattering:** queries that don't map cleanly to the role
vocabulary. "Someone who's good with historic homes" — no such role, but
some carpenters and masons specialize in restoration. BM25 handles this
weakly at best; embeddings handle it well.

**Approach:**
1. Pre-embed each crew's `bio + skills + certifications` using
   `text-embedding-3-small` (OpenAI) or a Groq-hosted embedding model.
2. Store the vector on the crew record. Atlas has vector search — add a
   second search index of type `vectorSearch`.
3. In the aggregation, add a `$vectorSearch` stage in parallel with
   `$search` (BM25), take a rank-fusion of both scores.
4. The parser prompt gets a new output field: `semanticQuery` — a rephrased
   version of the description optimized for embedding matching.

**Tradeoff:** Vectors cost storage + embedding-time on every crew update.
For 10k crew this is negligible; for 1M crew it starts to matter. Also, BM25
is more explainable ("we matched because their bio contains 'historic
restoration'"). Vectors are a black box. In the interview I'd argue for
hybrid (both signals) not replacement.

## Provider redundancy

If Groq is down, the whole product is degraded. Two mitigations:

- **Circuit breaker** in `getLLM()` — if 3 consecutive calls fail, skip LLM
  for 5 min and use the regex parser + template rationale. Users get service,
  quality drops.
- **Secondary provider config.** Env var `LLM_SECONDARY_BASE_URL` +
  `LLM_SECONDARY_API_KEY` + `LLM_SECONDARY_MODEL`. When circuit breaker
  trips, retry on secondary. Ollama Cloud, DeepInfra, and Together.ai all
  serve OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the same class of open models.

## What I'd build second (if we ship this MVP)

In order:

1. **Accept/reject button** on each result card + `matches.accepted` event
   logged — that's the training signal we need to move beyond keyword+geo
   scoring.
2. **Parser cache** — cheapest cost win.
3. **Availability windows** — biggest UX unlock (day-before crew swaps are
   the highest-pain use case per the brief).
4. **Auth + orgs** — needed before any real customer touches this.
5. **Vector rerank** — quality unlock for fuzzy queries.

# AGENTS.md — Construction Matchmaker

Canonical context file for anyone (human or agent) working in this repo.
This is the single source of truth for project shape, workflow, and
conventions. Deeper architectural detail lives in
[`/docs/architecture/`](./docs/architecture/README.md).

## What this is

A 4-hour timed-trial project for **Lemonlight**. A crew-matching micro-app
for general contractors: contractor types a one-sentence project
description → app returns 10 ranked crew matches from a 10,000-person
MongoDB database, each with an LLM-generated rationale.

The build will be demoed and pressed on during a 1-hour interview call. Every
technical decision must be defensible on latency, cost, and how it would
evolve past MVP. `/docs/architecture/future-work.md` prepares talking points
for the "how would you approach X" follow-up questions.

## Stack

| Layer | Choice |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Vite + React (single page, no state library) |
| Backend | Node 20 + Express + Mongoose |
| Database | MongoDB Atlas M0 (free), Atlas Search + `2dsphere` |
| LLM | **Groq** · `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, OpenAI-compatible SDK |
| Seed | `@faker-js/faker` + curated role/city vocabularies |
| Dev orchestration | `concurrently` at repo root |

Env-var contract (see `.env.example`):

- `MONGODB_URI` — Atlas connection string
- `GROQ_API_KEY` — Groq bearer token
- `GROQ_BASE_URL` — defaults to `https://api.groq.com/openai/v1`
- `GROQ_MODEL` — defaults to `openai/gpt-oss-120b`
- `PORT` — server port, defaults to 3001

## Repo layout

```
F:\web-clients\lemonlight\
├── AGENTS.md              # this file
├── CLAUDE.md              # thin pointer to AGENTS.md
├── .env                   # gitignored, user-populated
├── .env.example           # template
├── .gitignore
├── package.json           # root — dev scripts, concurrently
├── docs/
│   └── architecture/      # full architectural spec
│       ├── README.md      # index
│       ├── overview.md
│       ├── data-model.md
│       ├── search-flow.md
│       ├── llm-integration.md
│       ├── seeding.md
│       ├── api.md
│       ├── frontend.md
│       └── future-work.md
├── shared/
│   ├── roles.js           # 25 role vocabulary + skill pools + certs
│   └── cities.js          # ~100 US cities with lat/lng + population weight
├── server/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── index.js       # Express bootstrap
│   │   ├── db.js          # Mongoose connect
│   │   ├── llm.js         # OpenAI SDK factory pointed at Groq
│   │   ├── models/
│   │   │   ├── Crew.js
│   │   │   └── SearchLog.js
│   │   └── routes/
│   │       └── search.js  # POST /api/search
│   └── scripts/
│       ├── smoke.js       # verify Mongo + Groq
│       └── seed.js        # generate 10,000 crew records
└── client/
    ├── package.json
    ├── vite.config.js
    ├── index.html
    └── src/
        ├── main.jsx
        ├── App.jsx
        └── index.css
```

## Dev workflow

All commands are run from the repo root (`F:\web-clients\lemonlight`).

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run install:all` | Installs root + server + client deps |
| `npm run smoke` | Sanity-checks Mongo + Groq connectivity (~5s) |
| `npm run seed` | Wipes and reseeds `crew` collection with 10k records (~20s) |
| `npm run dev` | Runs server (`:3001`) + client (`:5173`) concurrently |
| `npm run server` | Runs server only |
| `npm run client` | Runs client only |

Typical bring-up on a fresh clone:

```
cp .env.example .env       # then fill MONGODB_URI + GROQ_API_KEY
npm run install:all
npm run smoke              # must pass before proceeding
npm run seed
npm run dev
# → open http://localhost:5173
```

## Where the meaningful code lives

- **The endpoint that does everything:** `server/src/routes/search.js`.
  Parse → aggregate → rationale → log. Read this file first.
- **The prompts:** in the same file. Extracted only if we grow past two.
- **The data model:** `server/src/models/Crew.js`,
  `server/src/models/SearchLog.js`.
- **The vocabularies:** `shared/roles.js` (roles + skills + certs),
  `shared/cities.js` (geo). Both `imported` by seed and server.

## Conventions

- **ES modules** everywhere (`"type": "module"` in server package.json,
  `.jsx` files client-side).
- **No dotenv package.** Server scripts use Node's built-in `--env-file=../.env`
  flag. Version pin: Node 20.6+ required.
- **No comments explaining WHAT code does.** Comments only for non-obvious
  WHY (hidden constraints, workarounds, invariants).
- **Fire-and-forget for `SearchLog.create`.** Logging must never block or
  fail a search.
- **Fallbacks over 500s.** LLM errors trigger regex-parser + template
  rationale, not user-visible failures. Mongo errors trigger a real 503.
- **Windows paths in tool calls.** Use full absolute paths with drive
  letter (`F:\web-clients\lemonlight\...`), backslashes OK.

## What's out of scope (per the brief)

- Auth
- Analytics beyond `SearchLog` persistence
- Cost optimization
- Date/time availability
- Any page beyond crew search

Each of these has an approach section in
[`/docs/architecture/future-work.md`](./docs/architecture/future-work.md) —
that's the go-to for the "how would you approach X" interview questions.

## Verification

The end-to-end verification steps live in
[`/docs/architecture/README.md`](./docs/architecture/README.md) and expand
each doc's own testing notes. Quick smoke test:

1. `npm run smoke` returns two green lines.
2. `npm run seed` reports `seeded 10000 crew records`.
3. `npm run dev`, browser to `http://localhost:5173`, run the demo query
   `"Need a licensed electrician in Austin for a kitchen rewire tomorrow"`,
   verify: results in <2s, top match is an electrician near Austin marked
   `Available`, the "Parsed as" panel shows the structured filter.
4. In Atlas: `db.searchlogs.find().sort({createdAt:-1}).limit(1)` — verify
   the query was logged.

## Doc <-> code sync rule

If you change a schema, prompt, endpoint, or the seed distribution, update
the matching file under `/docs/architecture/` **in the same commit**. Docs
drift is the enemy — this repo is small enough that keeping it in sync is
cheap and pays off on the interview call.

## Stack

| Layer | Choice |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Vite + React (single page, no state library) |
| Backend | Node 20 + Express + Mongoose |
| Database | MongoDB Atlas M0 (free), Atlas Search + `2dsphere` |
| LLM | **Groq** · `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, OpenAI-compatible SDK |
| Seed | `@faker-js/faker` + curated role/city vocabularies |
| Dev orchestration | `concurrently` at repo root |

Env-var contract (see `.env.example`):

- `MONGODB_URI` — Atlas connection string
- `GROQ_API_KEY` — Groq bearer token
- `GROQ_BASE_URL` — defaults to `https://api.groq.com/openai/v1`
- `GROQ_MODEL` — defaults to `openai/gpt-oss-120b`
- `PORT` — server port, defaults to 3001

├── AGENTS.md              # this file
├── CLAUDE.md              # thin pointer to AGENTS.md
├── .env                   # gitignored, user-populated

├── .gitignore

├── docs/
│   └── architecture/      # full architectural spec
│       ├── README.md      # index
│       ├── overview.md

├── server/

        └── index.css
```

## Dev workflow

All commands are run from the repo root (`F:\web-clients\lemonlight`).

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run install:all` | Installs root + server + client deps |
| `npm run smoke` | Sanity-checks Mongo + Groq connectivity (~5s) |
| `npm run seed` | Wipes and reseeds `crew` collection with 10k records (~20s) |
| `npm run dev` | Runs server (`:3001`) + client (`:5173`) concurrently |
| `npm run server` | Runs server only |
| `npm run client` | Runs client only |

Typical bring-up on a fresh clone:

```
cp .env.example .env       # then fill MONGODB_URI + GROQ_API_KEY
npm run install:all
npm run smoke              # must pass before proceeding
npm run seed
npm run dev
# → open http://localhost:5173
```

## Where the meaningful code lives

- **The endpoint that does everything:** `server/src/routes/search.js`.
  Parse → aggregate → rationale → log. Read this file first.
- **The prompts:** in the same file. Extracted only if we grow past two.
- **The data model:** `server/src/models/Crew.js`,
  `server/src/models/SearchLog.js`.
- **The vocabularies:** `shared/roles.js` (roles + skills + certs),
  `shared/cities.js` (geo). Both `imported` by seed and server.

## Conventions

- **ES modules** everywhere (`"type": "module"` in server package.json,
  `.jsx` files client-side).
- **No dotenv package.** Server scripts use Node's built-in `--env-file=../.env`
  flag. Version pin: Node 20.6+ required.
- **No comments explaining WHAT code does.** Comments only for non-obvious
  WHY (hidden constraints, workarounds, invariants).
- **Fire-and-forget for `SearchLog.create`.** Logging must never block or
  fail a search.
- **Fallbacks over 500s.** LLM errors trigger regex-parser + template
  rationale, not user-visible failures. Mongo errors trigger a real 503.
- **Windows paths in tool calls.** Use full absolute paths with drive
  letter (`F:\web-clients\lemonlight\...`), backslashes OK.

## What's out of scope (per the brief)

- Auth
- Analytics beyond `SearchLog` persistence
- Cost optimization
- Date/time availability
- Any page beyond crew search

Each of these has an approach section in
[`/docs/architecture/future-work.md`](./docs/architecture/future-work.md) —
that's the go-to for the "how would you approach X" interview questions.

## Verification

The end-to-end verification steps live in
[`/docs/architecture/README.md`](./docs/architecture/README.md) and expand
each doc's own testing notes. Quick smoke test:

1. `npm run smoke` returns two green lines.
2. `npm run seed` reports `seeded 10000 crew records`.
3. `npm run dev`, browser to `http://localhost:5173`, run the demo query
   `"Need a licensed electrician in Austin for a kitchen rewire tomorrow"`,
   verify: results in <2s, top match is an electrician near Austin marked
   `Available`, the "Parsed as" panel shows the structured filter.
4. In Atlas: `db.searchlogs.find().sort({createdAt:-1}).limit(1)` — verify
   the query was logged.

## Doc <-> code sync rule

If you change a schema, prompt, endpoint, or the seed distribution, update
the matching file under `/docs/architecture/` **in the same commit**. Docs
drift is the enemy — this repo is small enough that keeping it in sync is
cheap and pays off on the interview call.

- Task 4 — `Crew` + `SearchLog` Mongoose models + seed script (10k records)

content.text:
Install finished (both server + client landed clean). Now:

- **Headshots** — 10k images is impractical to generate individually (~$400 in Imagen calls, hours of runtime). I'll build a **pool of ~40 diverse construction-worker headshots** and assign deterministically per crew by hash + role/gender. Visually varied enough for the demo, cheap and fast.
- **Tailwind Plus / Tailwind UI** — that's the paid one; components are copy-paste from Tailwind's private portal, not npm. shadcn/ui (free, uses Tailwind under the hood) is what I'll wire up as the primary component system, and any Tailwind Plus JSX you drop in later will just work.
- **Tailwind version:** 3.4.x — stable and shadcn plug-and-play. If you'd rather Tailwind 4, say the word.

content.text:
Big pivot noted. Three architectural shifts stacked:

1. **Data model** — replace flat `skills: [string]` with structured `specializations: [{ skill, level 1–5, yearsInSpecialty }]` on a renamed `Subcontractor` collection.
2. **UI paradigm** — mobile-first fullscreen chat like Claude/ChatGPT mobile. LLM decides when to invoke a `search_subcontractors` tool; tool results render as rich cards inline.
3. **Ranking** — specialization level becomes a first-class scoring factor.

This does push us past the 4-hour budget the brief calls out, but the demo will be substantially stronger. Making these calls and moving:

- **Keep `/api/search`** (it's a hard requirement from the brief) as the underlying search primitive.
- **Add `/api/chat`** on top — takes conversation history, invokes Groq with function-calling, executes `search_subcontractors` server-side, returns synthesized response + tool results for the client to render as components.
- **Rename `crew` → `subcontractors`** everywhere to match your vocabulary.

Updating tasks and rewriting the affected architecture docs now, then continuing to code.

export function pickWeightedCity(rng = Math.random) {
  const total = CITIES.reduce((s, c) => s + c.weight, 0);
  let r = rng() * total;
  for (const c of CITIES) {
    r -= c.weight;
    if (r <= 0) return c;
  }
  return CITIES[CITIES.length - 1];
}

export function pickWeightedCity(rng = Math.random) {
  const total = CITIES.reduce((s, c) => s + c.weight, 0);
  let r = rng() * total;
  for (const c of CITIES) {
    r -= c.weight;
    if (r <= 0) return c;
  }
  return CITIES[CITIES.length - 1];
}
